query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of a ductility‐promoting refractory element to NbMoTaW to induce the in situ formation of dispersed, ductile B2 precipitates within its BCC matrix will improve room‐temperature ductility and enhance irradiation tolerance while keeping high‐temperature strength intact.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic, single‐phase BCC NbMoTaW that exhibits excellent properties at high temperatures (up to 1600 °C) but suffers from poor room‐temperature ductility and has only computationally inferred irradiation resistance.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor alloying addition (around 5–10 atomic percent) of a ductile refractory element (for example, titanium) into the NbMoTaW base composition to drive the formation of a dual-phase microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates embedded in a continuous BCC matrix.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing at room temperature to assess ductility, high-temperature tests up to approximately 1600 °C to confirm strength retention, and ion (helium) irradiation experiments at reactor-relevant temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an 'inverted' composite microstructure in which fine, ductile B2 precipitates are uniformly dispersed within the BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: The discrete B2 precipitates are expected to facilitate dislocation motion and act as effective defect sinks, thereby promoting plastic deformation at room temperature. These precipitate‐matrix interfaces can also enhance the recombination of irradiation-induced point defects (improving self-healing) and help control defect clustering, ultimately mitigating irradiation‐induced amorphization and blistering without degrading the high-temperature stability of the BCC phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is predicted to exhibit significantly improved room-temperature ductility (higher strain-to-failure) and reduced irradiation damage (e.g., smaller helium bubble sizes and less blistering) compared to untreated NbMoTaW, while retaining comparable high-temperature strength and phase stability.
generation.baseline: The unmodified, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW alloy with its known high-temperature performance and limited room-temperature plasticity.
generation.boundary: The benefits of the intervention are expected to be realized in the temperature range from room temperature up to ~1600 °C and under irradiation conditions typical of reactor environments (using helium-ion implantation at fluences similar to those reported in relevant studies).
generation.uncertainty: The optimal concentration of the ductility-promoting element and the precise precipitate morphology needed for the desired balance remain to be determined. Additionally, while the mechanism is supported by studies on dual-phase microstructures in refractory HEAs, the specific irradiation responses may vary with processing and microstructural homogeneity.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of samples: (a) standard equiatomic BCC NbMoTaW and (b) NbMoTaW modified by adding 5–10 at.% Ti (or a similar ductility-enhancing element) intended to produce a dual-phase BCC+B2 microstructure. Characterize the phase distribution using TEM/SEM and perform mechanical tests at room temperature and at high temperatures (up to 1600 °C). Additionally, subject both sets to helium-ion irradiation under controlled reactor-relevant conditions.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile or compressive ductility (strain-to-failure, yield strain)
High-temperature yield strength and phase stability assessments
Microstructural analysis to confirm the presence and distribution of B2 precipitates
Irradiation responses assessed by measuring features such as helium bubble size, density, and surface blistering via TEM or other imaging methods
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in room-temperature ductility and/or improved irradiation resistance (e.g., similar or larger helium bubble sizes, increased blistering) relative to the control NbMoTaW, or if its high-temperature strength is compromised, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Typically, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), comprising a two-phase ordered B2 + BCC microstructure, exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths, but poor ductility at room temperature, limiting their engineering application. The poor ductility is attributed to the continuous matrix being the ordered B2 phase in these alloys. This paper presents a novel approach to microstructural engineering of RHEAs to form an “inverted” BCC + B2 microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates dispersed within a continuous BCC matrix, resulting in improved room temperature compressive ductility, while maintaining high yield strength at both room and elevated temperature.

In 2004, Professor Yeh and his group published the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) []. He defined high-entropy alloys (HEAs) as having five or more major elements beneath 5–35 at.%, and minor elements below five at.%. In 2006, he also established four core effects of HEAs []: High-entropy, severe-lattices-distortion, sluggish-diffusion, and the cocktail effect. With the new concepts, scientists are able to develop and expand alloys without restrictions [,,,,]. Some HEAs have been found to have attractive properties on diffusion [], oxidation [], corrosion [], fatigue [], creep [], fracture toughness [], and elevated-temperature strength []. High-entropy superalloys (HESAs) [], eutectic HEAs (EHEAs) [], light-weight HEAs (LWHEAs) [], refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) [], etc. have been proposed and attract increased attention. In 2010, Senkov and Miracle first published RHEAs, MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW [,]. These two alloys possess body-centered cubic (BCC) structure and have excellent elevated-temperature yield strength which is around 400 MPa at 1600 °C.
